name: Postural Restoration Institute (PRI)

lead: Postural Restoration, developed by physical therapist Ron Hruska, uses breathing and positional exercises to correct body asymmetries. Users hope it leads to a more even, neutral and symmetrical posture.

The chain is breathing and asymmetry exercises, rebalanced alignment of the ribcage and pelvis, then a more neutral stance. Hruska founded the Postural Restoration Institute in 1999 to train health professionals. Published work is mostly case reports and physiology papers, and appearance outcomes have not been studied.

paras: PRI-trained therapists teach specific breathing patterns and positioning exercises, often with manual work, and give home routines to repeat. Programs run over multiple sessions.
No specific harms were documented in the sources reviewed. It is delivered by licensed professionals, and people with breathing or medical conditions may want to check with their clinician.

angle.text: PRI-trained therapists teach breathing and positional exercises aimed at correcting asymmetries, which users hope gives a more even, neutral posture. The path runs from breathing work to rebalanced ribcage and pelvis to better alignment. Published trials are few, and appearance outcomes have not been studied.

lead: Postural Restoration is a posture-based approach to physical therapy developed by physical therapist Ron Hruska in the early 1990s. In 1999 he founded the Postural Restoration Institute (PRI) in Lincoln, Nebraska, to train other health professionals [1]. Practitioners use manual techniques and non-manual exercises, many centred on breathing and pelvic position, to retrain asymmetrical movement patterns toward what they call neutrality [1].

For appearance, the draw is posture: people use PRI-style exercises hoping for more even shoulders, a less flared rib cage, a more neutral pelvis and a more upright, balanced stance, which changes how tall, lean and athletic someone looks. Advocates also say it improves breathing mechanics and movement, which can support better training [1].
The published literature on the method consists mainly of case reports, descriptions of individual exercises and small trials in athletes and in people with low back pain [2][3][4][5].
infobox: Posture and breathing-based physical therapy method
Diaphragm function, zone of apposition, asymmetry patterns

paras: Advocates say the body has built-in asymmetries, including a tendency to stand on the right leg, and that these show up in the ribs, pelvis and hips. PRI aims to restore neutrality and normal respiration through manual and non-manual exercises that reposition and retrain these patterns [1].

Breathing is central. Practitioners refer to the diaphragm's zone of apposition, where it attaches to the lower rib cage, and describe exercises such as the right sidelying respiratory left adductor pull back as ways to influence rib and pelvis alignment [1][3].

People interested in physique and posture use PRI exercises to address anterior pelvic tilt, rib flare and uneven shoulders, which can affect the silhouette of the waist, chest and back. Athletes also use the exercises for alignment before training. Practitioners describe the work as therapy delivered by trained clinicians, with home exercises prescribed afterwards.

A 2020 case report in the International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy described a collegiate volleyball player with chronic rotator cuff tendinopathy treated with PRI exercises aimed at pelvic alignment and breathing in place of her previous rehabilitation programme [2].

A 2019 randomized controlled trial in 25 physically active male students compared non-manual Postural Restoration exercises with traditional postural interventions on alignment, range of motion, symmetry, speed and power [4]. A 2021 randomized matched-subjects trial in 33 men with chronic low back pain compared NASM, PRI and combined exercise programmes for eight weeks and found no significant differences between groups in pain, disability or movement control [5]. A 2013 article described the right sidelying respiratory adductor pull back exercise and its rationale [3].

Wikipedia's article notes little strong evidence that any specific posture leads to better medical outcomes and lists a case study, an ethnography of the PRI community, a physiotherapist survey and classic respiratory mechanics papers among its references [1].

PRI is taught through courses to physical therapists, athletic trainers and strength coaches, and is used in sports performance settings [1]. Wikipedia also notes an ethnographic thesis on the method's practitioner community [1].
